touches.text: TICKET (a machine, and the class every kind of ticket inherits from; a first class object)

The abstract ticket owns what every kind shares: its birth (cast) and its three parts, each with one job: the plan (only what a builder builds from), the metadata and state (what gates and doors read and write as it moves), and the history (the append-only log). WHY: one job per part reduces confusion; a builder reads the plan and nothing else.

The ticket IS its own manager. It carries its workflow and status, and asks each gate whether it can transit. If refused, it gets itself back to design for fixing. If no handler is available to ask, it throws a trouble and waits until we decide. Design is CC and Akien. Akien, 2026-11-11, Q#85: "you and me. later there will be a specific agent for it, but that's so far off we're not even thinking about it now except 'after the outline is implemented'." So until then a refused ticket waits in the trouble lane, which both of us read when a session opens, and nothing posts to a design verb that no machine answers.

A ticket's code is a tool or machine; its life is data. All of its state is on disk, so anyone can instantiate it to talk to it, and any dialog is written to the relevant part of the ticket as it happens. To cross a gate the ticket asks that gate to queue it, sending only its fileref: devices/codemother/0/machines/<inspector>/queueme <fileref>. The gate instantiates the ticket from that fileref on its own side. A ticket instance then processes the pass or fail: on a pass it goes on to the next step, alerting the probes watching the gate (3.3.4.2); on a fail it asks design to queue it, the same way. Self-queuing is the abstract ticket's (3.3.2), so every kind inherits it and no caller queues a ticket on its behalf (Akien, same day: "that could be in the class, rather than the instance :) self queuing"). WHY: Akien, 2026-11-10: "now it has to send it's fileref over to the thing that will process it, and a new code instance created over there even tho it's the same thing... because that's good encapsulation. :)"
